title: A model of aesthetic appreciation and aesthetic judgments
authors: Helmut Leder, Benno Belke, Andries Oeberst, Dorothee Augustin
key_findings: Information-processing box model: perception, implicit memory integration, explicit classification, cognitive mastering, evaluation, with continuous emotional evaluation (as described in LederNadal2014)
Two outputs: aesthetic judgement and aesthetic emotion
Focus on modern art, where style recognition and meaning-making matter
practical_applications: Use the stages as a critique order: what is seen -> what it reminds of -> what kind/style it is -> what it means -> how well it was mastered
limitations: Original not read; content taken from abstract metadata and the 2014 retrospective
Mainly visual art, mainly modern art

title: Ten years of a model of aesthetic appreciation and aesthetic judgments: The aesthetic episode - Developments and challenges in empirical aesthetics
key_findings: Revised model: emotion is no longer external; early stages overlap in time
Experts use style to classify artworks by similarity, non-experts do not (Augustin & Leder 2006); non-experts like representational more than abstract art
Context effects: labels 'gallery' vs 'computer' change liking and brain activity (Kirk et al. 2009); museum viewing raises liking, interest and viewing time vs lab (Brieber et al. 2014)
Museum viewing time per artwork: mean 27 s, median 17 s (Smith & Smith 2001); median 11 s (Troendle et al. 2012)
Shift away from single-factor explanations (complexity, arousal, prototypicality) to interaction of cognition and affect; Berlyne's arousal framework dominated 1970s
practical_applications: Context and framing are part of the work: caption, venue and label change judgement
Design for seconds of attention, not minutes
limitations: Authors' own review; many cited studies small lab samples
Lab vs real-world gap acknowledged

title: Move me, astonish me... delight my eyes and brain: The Vienna Integrated Model of top-down and bottom-up processes in Art Perception (VIMAP) and corresponding affective, evaluative, and neurophysiological correlates
authors: Matthew Pelowski, Patrick S. Markey, Michael Forster, Gernot Gerger, Helmut Leder
key_findings: Integrates bottom-up artwork-driven processing with top-down processes by which viewers adapt or change
Built around three processing checks that delineate outcomes from mundane to moving, disturbing or transformative
Addresses chills, awe, thrills, sublime and aesthetic vs everyday emotion; links stages to brain networks
practical_applications: Plan for mismatch: a piece that breaks expectation needs a route to resolution or it ends in rejection
limitations: Theoretical; many predictions untested
Brain mappings are hypotheses

title: Fechner (1866): The Aesthetic Association Principle - A Commented Translation
authors: Stefan A. Ortlieb, Werner A. Kuegel, Claus-Christian Carbon
key_findings: Fechner (1801-1887) founded empirical aesthetics ('aesthetics from below')
Aesthetic choices are largely shaped by the observer's learning history (associative factor) rather than formal properties (direct factor)
Commentators: role of content and personal meaning still underrated in empirical aesthetics
practical_applications: Ask what the audience associates with a colour/material/motif before judging its form
limitations: Thought experiments, not data; read abstract only

title: Exposure and affect: Overview and meta-analysis of research, 1968-1987
key_findings: (secondary) ~208 experiments, r about .26; effect stronger for complex than simple stimuli and when many stimuli are shown; stronger without awareness/recognition
practical_applications: Repeated brand assets (colour, shape, motif) build liking, but only with variation
limitations: Not read; numbers from secondary summaries only
Lab stimuli

title: A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking
authors: R. Matthew Montoya, Robert S. Horton, Jack L. Vevea, Martyna Citkowicz, Elissa A. Lauber
key_findings: 268 curve estimates from 81 articles: positive slope + negative quadratic = inverted-U between exposure and liking
Inverted-U for visual (not auditory) stimuli, for exposure durations <10 s and >1 min
Existing models of mere exposure do not adequately account for the findings
practical_applications: Familiarity helps up to a point, then wears out: rotate executions of a recurring format
limitations: Lab stimuli; abstract only

title: Gustave Caillebotte, French Impressionism, and mere exposure
key_findings: 132 Impressionist images; cultural exposure indexed by 4,232 appearances in 980 Cornell library books
Adult preferences correlated with image frequency, not with recognition, complexity or prototypicality; children's preferences not correlated with frequency
Lab exposure interacted with prior cultural exposure; conclusion: mere exposure helps maintain an artistic canon
practical_applications: What a culture sees repeatedly becomes 'good taste': reference libraries shape the eye, so curate them deliberately
limitations: Only high-quality works tested (critique by Meskin et al. 2013)
Correlational for cultural exposure

title: Mere Exposure to Bad Art
authors: Aaron Meskin, Mark Phelan, Margaret Moore, Matthew Kieran
key_findings: (press/blog summaries) Repeated exposure to Thomas Kinkade paintings lowered liking, while Millais ratings did not drop
Authors: exposure does not operate independently of artistic quality
practical_applications: Repetition amplifies whatever quality is there: repeating a weak template makes it worse
limitations: Read only press/blog summaries; sample size reported differently (57 vs >100)
Student sample, UK

title: Changing Highbrow Taste: From Snob to Omnivore
authors: Richard A. Peterson, Roger M. Kern
key_findings: US survey data: highbrows increasingly 'omnivorous' (open to middle and lowbrow forms), via cohort replacement and change within cohorts during the 1980s
Challenges Bourdieu's assumption that elite and popular taste exclude each other
practical_applications: Mixing high and popular references is itself a status signal now; don't assume 'premium' means only highbrow codes
limitations: Read via search summaries; omnivore concept criticised as flexible/ambiguous and possibly still a form of distinction

title: Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste (trans. Richard Nice; French orig. 1979)
key_findings: (via secondary) Taste is learned in childhood, tied to habitus and cultural capital, and works as a class marker; 'taste classifies, and it classifies the classifier'
Dominant 'aesthetic disposition' (form over function) vs popular aesthetic expecting function; data from 1960s French surveys with correspondence analysis
practical_applications: Treat 'good taste' claims as social positioning; ask whose taste a brief is coded for
limitations: Book not read; France 1960s data; later critiques (omnivore thesis)

title: Distinction (book) - Wikipedia
key_findings: Summary of Bourdieu's argument: cultural capital, habitus, symbolic violence, working-class functional aesthetic vs aesthetic gaze; surveys 1963 (Kodak) and 1967 (taste)
practical_applications: Orientation only
limitations: Community encyclopedia; lists no criticisms

title: Dewey's Aesthetics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Art as Experience (1934): aesthetic experience = 'an experience' with inception, development, fulfilment, vs inchoate/anaesthetic experience
Continuity of art and everyday life; critique of the 'museum conception of art'; enemies of the aesthetic are the humdrum and mechanical routine
Doing and undergoing; functional (not tick-tock) rhythm; audience re-creates the work; 'science states meanings; art expresses them'
Critiques: Carroll (works like 4'33'' don't fit), Shusterman (concept too slippery), Saito (everyday aesthetics)
practical_applications: A post/clip should be one complete experience with build and resolution; rhythm = each beat carries the previous one forward
limitations: Philosophy, not empirical

title: Japanese Aesthetics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), rev. 2023-12-06
key_findings: Concepts: mono no aware (pathos of impermanence), wabi (understated austere beauty), sabi (rustic patina, solitude), yugen (mysterious depth by suggestion), iki (refined urban style), kire (cut-continuity)
Cautions: Japanese aesthetics as a discipline began in the 19th century; Kuki's iki uses European phenomenology; concepts were appropriated for nationalism
practical_applications: Use these words only with their documented meaning; 'wabi-sabi' is not a filter preset
limitations: Philosophical overview; not a preference study

title: Good design - Dieter Rams's ten principles for good design (Vitsoe)
key_findings: Ten principles: innovative, useful, aesthetic, understandable, unobtrusive, honest, long-lasting, thorough, environmentally friendly, as little design as possible ('less, but better')
Formulated late 1970s in reaction to an 'impenetrable confusion of forms, colours and noises'
practical_applications: Use as a craft checklist for restraint and honesty, not as science
limitations: Industrial-design ethos; not empirically tested as rules

title: Avant-Garde and Kitsch (Partisan Review 6:5, 1939)
key_findings: (via secondary) Kitsch as ersatz culture that copies the surface effects of art; 'vicarious experience and faked sensations'
Greenberg later distanced himself from parts of the essay
practical_applications: Kitsch test: does the image give the effect without the work that earns it?
limitations: Original scan not read; summaries via Wikipedia/Britannica

title: Kitsch and Art
key_findings: Three conditions of kitsch: (1) emotionally charged stock themes triggering unreflective emotion, (2) instantly identifiable objects/themes, (3) does not substantially enrich associations
practical_applications: Use the three conditions as a cliché detector for emotional content (sunsets, babies, couples)
limitations: Book not read; conditions from publisher blurb and citing papers

title: A Functional Model of Kitsch and Art: Linking Aesthetic Appreciation to the Dynamics of Social Motivation
key_findings: Kitsch = fluent, quick positive gratification; art = disfluent, effortful, insight; preference linked to safety vs arousal/autonomy motives
Threat, prevention focus, sad mood -> preference for familiar/fluent; safety and self-efficacy -> appetite for novelty
Art training reduces preference for conventional harmony (several cited studies)
practical_applications: Comfort content (kitsch-like fluency) and challenging content serve different moods; match to audience state
limitations: Theoretical, largely untested as a whole; ~60% of text read

title: Stronger shared taste for natural aesthetic domains than for artifacts of human culture
authors: Edward A. Vessel, Natalia Maurer, Alexander H. Denker, G. Gabrielle Starr
key_findings: Agreement high for faces and natural landscapes; strong individual differences for exterior/interior architecture and artworks
Within-subject: agreement higher for landscapes than exterior architecture, with equal reliability
practical_applications: Nature/faces: crowd-pleasing defaults work; designed artefacts and art styles: expect split audiences, test with target group
limitations: Western online samples; photographs

title: Individual Aesthetic Preferences for Faces Are Shaped Mostly by Environments, Not Genes
authors: Laura Germine, Richard Russell, P. Matthew Bronstad, et al., Jeremy B. Wilmer
key_findings: 547 MZ + 214 DZ twin pairs: individual face preferences A = 22%, C = 0%, E (unshared environment + error) = 78%
Individual taste for faces reliably measurable and driven by personal life history, not family
practical_applications: Personal taste is real and learned; a reviewer's private face/style preference is not a universal rule
limitations: E includes measurement error; faces only

title: Quantifying Visual Preferences Around the World
key_findings: 2.4 million ratings, ~40,000 participants, 430 websites
Peak-appeal colourfulness 6.1/9 on average but 3.6-7.6 across groups; complexity peaks 2.5-4.8
Women liked colourful sites more; 41+ liked more colourful/complex; higher education -> less colourful/complex
Neighbouring countries similar; Finland/Russia lowest complexity and colourfulness; former Yugoslav countries highly colourful; North < South Europe in colourfulness
practical_applications: There is no universal 'clean' level: set colour/complexity for the target group and test
limitations: Websites only; volunteer LabintheWild sample; causes speculative; Thailand not reported separately

title: Visual and Auditory Aesthetic Preferences Across Cultures
authors: Harin Lee, Eline Van Geert, Elif Celen, Raja Marjieh, Pol van Rijn, Minsu Park, Nori Jacoby
key_findings: 401,403 judgements from 4,835 participants in 10 countries across shape, curvature, colour, harmony, melody
Symmetry preferred everywhere; squares (1:1) peak; no preference peak at the golden ratio in any country
Japanese participants uniquely preferred straight lines; melody most culturally variable; geographic proximity not always similar
practical_applications: Symmetry is a safe universal; colour ratios, curvature and melody need local testing; drop golden-ratio claims
limitations: Conference paper/preprint; online panel; Thailand not among the countries

title: Culture and aesthetic preference: comparing the attention to context of East Asians and Americans
authors: Takahiko Masuda, Richard Gonzalez, Letty Kwan, Richard E. Nisbett
key_findings: Traditional East Asian art predominantly context-inclusive, Western art object-focused (museum archives)
Contemporary East Asians draw landscapes and take portraits with more context; preferences for portraits follow the same pattern
practical_applications: For East Asian audiences, test wider framings with environment, not only tight product isolation
limitations: Japan/US samples mainly; Thailand not tested; abstract only

title: Cross-cultural empirical aesthetics
authors: Jiajia Che, Xiaolei Sun, Victor Gallardo, Marcos Nadal
key_findings: Critical review of whether processes underlying aesthetic preference are universal; field dominated by Western samples (as cited by later papers)
practical_applications: Treat Western findings as hypotheses for Thai audiences
limitations: Not read; abstract-level information only

title: Learning Concepts and Categories: Is Spacing the 'Enemy of Induction'?
key_findings: Learning painters' styles: interleaved (spaced) study beat massed study for classifying new paintings (Exp 1a .61 vs .35, d = 0.99)
Learners judged massing more effective even after their own test showed the opposite
practical_applications: Train taste by mixing references from several styles side by side, not one style at a time; don't trust the feeling of fluency
limitations: Student samples; style recognition, not quality judgement

title: Perceptual learning
key_findings: Four mechanisms: attention weighting, stimulus imprinting, differentiation, unitization
Draws on expert/novice and cross-cultural evidence
practical_applications: Taste training = learning where to look (weights), what differences exist (differentiation), seeing configurations as units
limitations: Read via abstract snippets and SEP summary

title: Perceptual Learning (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Explains Goldstone's four mechanisms with examples (wine, /r/-/l/, expert athletes' gaze)
Ransom (2022): attention weighting and imprinting let experts perceive aesthetic properties; Nanay (2017): mere exposure undermines the argument from agreement
Debate whether training changes perception itself or only judgement (Fodor sceptical)
practical_applications: Expert eye is partly perceptual and domain-bound; train it on the domain you work in
limitations: Philosophical review

title: Bias in perceptual learning
key_findings: Perceptual learning benefits are tied to the learner's narrow interests and training environment; when either changes, benefits can become liabilities (often temporary)
practical_applications: An eye trained on one platform/style can misjudge another: re-calibrate with fresh references when switching format
limitations: Abstract only

title: Beauty in the Eye of Expert and Nonexpert Beholders: A Study in the Appraisal of Art
authors: Paul Hekkert, Piet C. W. van Wieringen
key_findings: Experts and non-experts agreed on originality but not on craftsmanship or quality
Originality-quality correlation r = .88 for experts vs .40 for non-experts
practical_applications: Experts reward originality much more than general audiences: decide which audience you design for
limitations: Abstract via search summary only; URL is the JSTOR stable link pattern and DOI not confirmed
Dutch sample of young artists' slides

title: What makes an art expert? Emotion and evaluation in art appreciation
authors: Helmut Leder, Gernot Gerger, David Brieber, Norbert Schwarz
key_findings: Experts showed attenuated emotional reactions (less extreme valence, less corrugator EMG) and liked negative art more; same for IAPS control pictures
practical_applications: Experts tolerate (and like) difficult/negative content more than general viewers: don't use a designer's comfort as proxy for audience comfort
limitations: Lab study, Vienna; abstract only

title: Design aesthetics: principles of pleasure in design
key_findings: Four principles: maximum effect for minimum means, unity in variety, MAYA (most advanced yet acceptable; Loewy), optimal match across senses
Typicality and novelty highly negatively correlated but not perfectly, so novelty can be raised while keeping typicality (Hekkert et al. 2003)
Agreement expected for unity-in-variety; MAYA leads to individual differences because typicality/novelty depend on exposure
practical_applications: Design-taste checklist: economy, unity with variety, novelty within the category frame, all senses saying the same thing
limitations: Theoretical/evolutionary framing; evidence mostly visual product studies

title: 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
authors: Paul Hekkert, Dirk Snelders, Piet C. W. van Wieringen
key_findings: Typicality and novelty jointly predict preference for products (telephones, teakettles, cars) - as summarised in Hekkert2006
practical_applications: Push novelty only as far as the category stays recognisable
limitations: Not re-read this session beyond Hekkert2006 summary

title: Putting the Art in Artificial: Aesthetic Responses to Computer-generated Art
authors: Rebecca Chamberlain, Caitlin Mullin, Bram Scheerlinck, Johan Wagemans
key_findings: Bias against art categorised as computer-generated; explicit prejudice driven largely by beliefs about what algorithms can produce; reproduced for robotic art
practical_applications: Viewers' beliefs about the maker change value; show human intent/process when AI is involved
limitations: Pre-diffusion era; abstract via search

title: Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art
key_findings: 4M+ artworks, ~53,000 artists, ~5,800 AI adopters; difference-in-differences
Productivity up (~50% in adoption month); favourites per view up from ~2% to ~3% by month 6
Average content novelty and average + peak visual novelty declined (convergence to a preferred style); peak content novelty marginally rose
Artists rewarded for exploring new concepts with AI, penalised for using AI to explore new visual styles
practical_applications: The 'AI look' is measurable convergence of visual style: put novelty in the idea and keep a deliberate house style
limitations: Observational; one platform; adoption detected by tags; process not observed

title: Generative AI and Creativity: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Niklas Holzner, Sebastian Maier, Stefan Feuerriegel
key_findings: 28 studies, 8,214 participants: GenAI alone vs humans g = -0.05 (ns); humans+GenAI vs humans alone g = 0.27; diversity of ideas g = -0.86 (homogenisation)
practical_applications: Use AI to raise individual output but add explicit diversity steps (many directions, human selection, references outside the model)
limitations: Preprint; mostly text/ideation tasks, not images

title: The Algorithmic Gaze of Image Quality Assessment: An Audit and Trace Ethnography of the LAION-Aesthetics Predictor
authors: Jordan Taylor, William Agnew, Maarten Sap, Sarah E. Fox, Haiyi Zhu
key_findings: LAION-Aesthetics Predictor (CLIP + MLP) curated LAION-Aesthetics used to pre-train early Stable Diffusion
Favours realistic landscapes, cityscapes and portraits, Western and Japanese 2-D art; abstract art and 3-D artefacts score low; no African/Native American/Oceanic MET object scored >= 6.5
Captions mentioning women more likely kept at 6.5+; men and LGBTQ+ more likely filtered out
Training ratings from English-speaking photographers (AVA) and Western AI enthusiasts; model built largely by one person's choices
practical_applications: Generic 'AI beauty' partly comes from what aesthetic filters rewarded: realistic, pretty, Western-photographic; counter it deliberately
limitations: Preprint to appear at FAccT 2026; one predictor; correlational caption analysis

title: AVA: A large-scale database for aesthetic visual analysis
authors: Naila Murray, Luca Marchesotti, Florent Perronnin
key_findings: 250,000+ images with aesthetic scores, 60+ semantic labels and photographic style labels
practical_applications: Know that most aesthetic-score models are trained on photo-contest ratings
limitations: Not read; abstract via search

title: NIMA: Neural Image Assessment
key_findings: Predicts the distribution of 1-10 ratings rather than one mean; AVA ~255,000 photos, ~200 raters each; about half of AVA photos have rating SD > 1.4
practical_applications: High rater disagreement is built into 'aesthetic score': use scores to filter technical junk, not to pick the creative winner
limitations: Search summary only (Google Research blog + arXiv listing)

title: Taming Preference Mode Collapse via Directional Decoupling Alignment (arXiv:2512.24146)
key_findings: Names 'preference mode collapse': reward-driven fine-tuning of text-to-image models pushes outputs toward narrow high-scoring styles (e.g. monolithic styles, overexposure); proposes DivGenBench
practical_applications: Expect default outputs of preference-tuned models to converge; prompt and select against the default
limitations: Preprint; authors not recorded; search summary only

title: A History of Manners and Civility in Thailand (Introduction: Manners and the Thai Habitus)
key_findings: Official Thai conception of manners linked to deference, discipline and orderliness (khwam riap roi)
Kepner: 'nearly obsessive concern with how people look, move, stand, walk, sit, dress'; Van Esterik: kala thesa = heightened awareness of social context guiding dress, talk, action
Uses Bourdieu/Elias habitus; Thai near-equivalent jarit
practical_applications: Thai visual taste for public-facing work: neatness, appropriateness to occasion (kalatesa), respect cues - test before going 'raw/messy'
limitations: Read only the publisher excerpt (introduction); history of manners, not a preference study; year not confirmed

title: Aesthetic Experience from Thai Colors
key_findings: Documents traditional Thai pigments (names, largely obsolete production), links colours to Buddhist symbolism (e.g. red/vermillion and heaven), builds a colour reference and three installations
practical_applications: Source for a Thai traditional palette with meanings, instead of generic 'Thai = gold + red'
limitations: Practice-based research; abstract only

title: The Taste Gap: Ira Glass on the Secret of Creative Success (The Marginalian)
key_findings: Glass: beginners have good taste but early work falls short; 'everybody goes through that'; remedy is a large volume of work on deadlines
practical_applications: Use volume + deadlines + comparison to close the gap; not a research finding
limitations: Anecdotal craft advice; original interview date/place not given on the page

title: Hume's Aesthetics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Standard of taste = joint verdict of true judges: strong sense, delicacy, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice (read 2026-11-25 for M06)
practical_applications: Basis of critique protocol
limitations: Reused from M06; not re-read this session

title: Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Judgement of beauty: disinterested, claims universal validity without rules; free vs adherent beauty (read 2026-11-25 for M06)
practical_applications: Commercial work = adherent beauty, judged against purpose
limitations: Reused from M06; not re-read this session
